<explanation>
Based on the file tree and the README, the Pkl project is a multi-module system that implements a “configuration as code” language with a rich set of tooling, validation, and integrations. The project is organized as a Gradle multi-module build (with buildSrc, several subprojects, and many “pkl-…” modules), and it also includes documentation generators, CLI tools, language bindings (for Java, Kotlin, Go, Swift, etc.), integration with build systems (such as a Gradle plugin), standard library modules, and even a server/executor component.

How to break it down and design an accurate system architecture diagram:

1. Identify major components (nodes) in the system:
 • Core Language Engine (pkl-core): This is the heart of the system which includes the parser (ANTLR and custom parsing code), AST (abstract syntax tree) construction, evaluator and various utility classes. It also handles the runtime aspects such as module resolution, security management, and execution.
 • Standard Library (stdlib): These modules provide built-in functionality. They supply the default modules (for JSON, YAML, math, XML, etc.) that the Pkl language can import.
 • CLI and Interpreters (pkl-cli, pkl-executor, pkl-server): The command-line interface (pkl-cli) provides an interactive or scriptable way to run Pkl programs. The executor and server subprojects further support remote or embedded execution, with a SPI design that allows for different execution strategies.
 • Code Generation Modules (pkl-codegen-java, pkl-codegen-kotlin, pkl-commons-cli): These components generate code in target languages from Pkl configurations. They depend on the core engine to resolve information and then produce artifacts (e.g., Java or Kotlin code).
 • Build System Integration (pkl-gradle): This module integrates Pkl into Gradle builds. It contains tasks and extensions (like “CodeGenTask” or “EvalTask”) that enable projects to use Pkl as part of their build pipelines.
 • Documentation System (pkl-doc): This module uses the core information and the documentation of Pkl packages to generate human-readable documentation (HTML, Markdown) for language reference and package documentation.
 • Additional Tools and Plugins (pkl-tools, pkl-lsp, IDE integrations, etc.): These support ecosystem integrations; they are separate repositories but tie into the overall Pkl ecosystem.

2. Determine the relationships and data flows between components:
 • The CLI (or Gradle plugin) accepts a Pkl source file from the user and hands it off to the Core Engine.
 • The Core Engine (pkl-core) parses the source, constructs an AST, applies validations, resolves modules, and executes or interprets the configuration.
 • The Standard Library modules are imported by the Core Engine as built-in modules.
 • Code generation modules take the processed AST or resolved module information from the Core and emit source code for target languages.
 • The Documentation module reads package definitions (often packaged as Pkl packages) and uses code and comments to generate docs.
 • The Executor/Server modules enable the Pkl process to be run in a dedicated process or container (e.g., remote execution or tests).

3. Architectural patterns/design principles:
 • Modular design with clear layer separations: core language processing is separated from tooling and integrations.
 • Dependency inversion: many modules (e.g., code generators, documentation generators, Gradle plugin) depend on abstractions provided by pkl-core.
 • Plugin architecture: The presence of SPI interfaces (e.g., in pkl-executor/spi) makes it easy to extend or swap out components.
 • Build system integration: Gradle is used as the build orchestration tool with custom tasks defined in modules such as pkl-gradle and buildSrc.
 • Extensive testing and benchmarking: Directories like “bench” and “pkl-commons-test” indicate that performance and correctness are continuously monitored.

4. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram:
 a. Draw nodes for each major module (e.g., Core Engine, StdLib, CLI, Codegen, Gradle Plugin, Documentation, Executor/Server).
 b. For each component, list key technologies or responsibilities (e.g., the Core Engine node could be annotated “Parser, AST, Evaluator, Module Resolver”).
 c. Draw directional arrows showing flow:
  – User input flows into the CLI/Gradle Plugin.
  – The CLI invokes the Core Engine.
  – The Core Engine imports libraries from the StdLib.
  – Code generation tools and documentation generators pull from the Core Engine.
  – The Executor/Server components receive configurations from pkl-core for execution.
 d. Use distinct colors or shapes to represent layers:
  – For instance, use one color or shape for “language processing” (pkl-core, stdlib), another for “interfaces” (CLI, Gradle plugin, server/executor) and another for “tooling” (code generators, docs).
 e. Clearly label inter-module dependencies with annotations (for example, “invokes”, “depends on”, “generates from”, etc).

5. Additional details to include:
 • Indicate the use of Gradle as the build system with an arrow from “buildSrc and Gradle configuration” to all subprojects.
 • Highlight testing and benchmarking as peripheral components that validate all layers.
 • Mention that each repository (CLI, core, docs, etc.) is part of the same ecosystem and shares common utilities (e.g., those in pkl-commons and pkl-commons-cli).

In summary, your detailed diagram should be structured with clear compartmentalization:
 – At the center place the Core Engine (pkl-core) together with the StdLib.
 – Surrounding that, show the interfaces like the CLI, Executor/Server, and Build Integration components.
 – Off to the side, list auxiliary tooling (code generators and documentation generators) that hook into the core.
 – Clearly mark the multi-layer dependency and data flow arrows between components.
Use clear labels, directional arrows for call flows, and appropriate color or shapes to differentiate system layers. This comprehensive diagram will serve as an accurate high-level overview of the architectural design of the Pkl project.

This should provide the level of detail needed for a principal software engineer to understand the overall architecture and its key components.
</explanation>
